tagline.text: Antique's forest of water, home to Rafflesia and rare birds

location.label: Location
location.text: Sibalom, Antique (a protected forest spanning 16 barangays)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–3,500 (per person, estimate for transport, guide and meals; confirm locally)

children.text: Sibalom Natural Park is a natural park of about 5,511 hectares in Sibalom, Antique, designated in 2000. In the forests around Mount Porras you can find the giant Rafflesia flower, 76 bird species and rare animals such as the Visayan spotted deer, and the park also supplies drinking water to five municipalities.

Sibalom Natural Park is a protected area in the municipality of Sibalom, Antique, on the west side of Panay. According to Wikipedia it covers 5,511.47 hectares across 16 barangays and is managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). It began on June 28, 1990 as the Tipulu-an Mau-it Rivers Watershed Forest Reserve (7,737 hectares) and was proclaimed a natural park on April 23, 2000. The terrain centers on Mount Porras (about
, 800 ft), rising in the middle of the park amid low mountains and hills.

The value of this place lies in its forest and water. The forest mixes mild montane forest, lowland forest, some bushland and open cogon grassland, and about 5,000 hectares of forest stretch from Mount Porras to Mount Igmatindog. Of this, about 672 hectares are undisturbed forest and about 4,223 hectares are a reforestation site roughly 50 years old. As a watershed forest holding the Tipulu-an and Mao-it rivers, tributaries of the Sibalom River, the park supplies drinking water to five municipalities and irrigates about 5,500 hectares of rice fields.

Its biodiversity stands out even in the Philippines. Trees include dipterocarps such as white lauan and apitong and fruit trees such as antipolo and malapaho, and the giant flower Rafflesia speciosa, discovered on Mount Porras in 2002, blooms in the park. Seventy-six bird species have been recorded, 28 of them endemic to the Philippines, including the Negros bleeding-heart, Walden's hornbill, the Visayan hornbill, the blue-naped parrot and the eastern grass owl. Endemic animals include the Visayan spotted deer, the Visayan warty pig, the giant Visayan frog and the Philippine sailfin lizard. Semi-precious stones such as agate, jasper and onyx are said to occur in the riverbeds.
For travelers this is an ecological destination rather than a sightseeing spot. Wikipedia places the park about
36 km
east of San Jose de Buenavista and about
140 km

west of Iloilo City, and says it serves as a corridor between the Northwest Panay Peninsula Natural Park and the Central Panay Mountain Range. Little is confirmed about trails, how to enter and fees, so this guide concentrates on geography and nature and advises you to contact the local DENR office (PENRO) and the Sibalom municipal tourism desk before visiting. When planning, remember that the park lies between Antique's inland mountains and its west-coast towns. You could start from Iloilo, pass through the coastal church towns, spend a day in Sibalom, and continue the next day toward San Jose or north to Tibiao.

A Rafflesia discovered on Mount Porras in 2002 and the symbolic plant of this park. The flower blooms only for a short period and the timing varies from year to year, so it is hard to predict. If you want to see it, check bloom news with the local management office beforehand.

Of the 76 bird species, 28 are endemic to the Philippines. Well-known birds on record include Walden's hornbill, the Visayan hornbill, the blue-naped parrot and the Negros bleeding-heart, which makes the park attractive to birdwatchers. Early morning is best.

Endemic species such as the Visayan spotted deer, the Visayan warty pig, the giant Visayan frog and the Philippine sailfin lizard live here. Wildlife is not easy to spot, so the trick is to walk quietly with a guide.
About 5,000 hectares of forest stretch from Mount Porras (about
) at the center of the park to Mount Igmatindog. It is a low mountain, so it is not a high-altitude climb, but trail marking may be poor, so a guide is needed.

The Tipulu-an and Mao-it rivers flow into the Sibalom River, supply drinking water to five municipalities and irrigate about 5,500 hectares of rice fields. Walking here knowing that the villages below depend on this forest changes how you see the protected area.
About 4,223 hectares are a reforestation site about 50 years old. Primary forest and restored forest are mixed, so you can see a forest growing back with your own eyes.
Semi-precious minerals such as agate, jasper and onyx are said to occur in the riverbeds. Collecting stones and minerals inside a protected area may be prohibited, so look but do not take.
Unlike an ordinary Antique trip along the coastal road, here you see inland rice fields, villages and foothills. It is close to Sibalom town, so it fits easily into a one-day plan.
Leave Sibalom town or San Jose, register your visit at the DENR office (PENRO) or the town hall, and find a guide.
Meet your guide at the village at the park entrance and enter the forest trail. Birds are most active early.
Rest by a stream, have lunch and look around the riverbed and forest scenery.
Descend, rest in the village and head back to town.
Trails inside the park and areas open to visitors may change with local circumstances. Be sure to check the latest information before you set out.
Set out at dawn and go to a spot where you can watch birds in the early morning.
Observe plants, insects and animal signs along the forest trail and listen to your guide's explanations.
Have lunch in the village and talk with local residents about conservation work.
Return to Sibalom town and look around the market and the area near the church.
If a Rafflesia is in bloom, your guide may be able to take you to it. Do not go close to touch or pick the flower.
Direct flights run daily from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), taking about
1 hour 10 minutes
. Schedules change by season, so check when booking.
San Jose, the capital of Antique, has an airport (EUQ) that has had Manila flights, but there are few of them, so check whether they currently operate.
Buses and vans toward San Jose and Libertad leave from a terminal in the Molo district of Iloilo City. Sibalom is a town on this route on the side nearer San Jose.
The trip from Iloilo to San Jose is generally said to take
2–3 hours
, and Sibalom is reached before that. Confirm fares locally.
Bus schedules change often, so check at the terminal.
According to Wikipedia the park is about
36 km
east of San Jose de Buenavista. From Sibalom town you enter the park-entrance village by tricycle, jeepney or motorcycle taxi (habal-habal).
There may be unpaved sections, so travel can take longer after rain.
Inside the park there are only walking trails, and it is safer to move with a guide.
Check the areas open to visitors and trail conditions with the DENR office.
The park is large and may have several entrances, so agree with your guide in advance which entrance you will use and where you will come down.

The dry season, December to May, is the best time for walking. In the rainy season streams swell, forest trails get slippery, and leeches and mosquitoes increase, which can make a visit hard. At midday you sweat a lot even under the trees, so walk mostly in the morning and come down early in the afternoon.

Rafflesia blooms briefly and is hard to predict. If seeing the flower is your goal, ask the local management office about bloom conditions beforehand, and go ready to enjoy the birds and forest even if you miss it. Birds are most active in the early morning.

It is realistic to stay in Sibalom town or in San Jose de Buenavista, the provincial capital. Both are small towns with few hotel choices, so book ahead, and ask your guide whether a homestay is available in the park-entrance village. Prices and reviews change by season, so check the latest information. Staying in town also helps with an early-morning birdwatching start. Arrange early-morning transport the day before through your lodging or your guide.

Eat at restaurants and markets in town. In Antique you can easily find ordinary Filipino food such as grilled meat and fish dishes and chicken inasal, and in this rice-growing area a meal of rice with fresh vegetables is common. There are no restaurants in the forest, so bring your own lunch and water and take all your trash back with you.
Before your visit, ask the Sibalom town hall or the local DENR office whether visits are allowed and what the fees are.
Walk the forest trails with a guide, and move slowly and quietly if you want to see birds and animals.
Bring binoculars, insect repellent, a hat, long sleeves and spare socks.
Pack shoes or sandals that can get wet for stream crossings.
Do not collect plants, stones or insects, and leave no trash.
Do not step on or touch a Rafflesia; take photos only from the distance your guide sets.
Bring plenty of cash. There are almost no ATMs in rural villages.
Phone signal may be weak in places, so download offline maps.
After your visit, greet villagers, and help the guide and the village keep up conservation work with a small tip or by buying local products. Ask permission before photographing people's faces.
This park is not a place with well-developed tourist facilities. Trail and fee information could not be confirmed, so be sure to check the latest notice with the DENR office before visiting.
A Rafflesia in bloom is not guaranteed. Go prepared not to be disappointed if there are no flowers.
In the rainy season streams can rise suddenly and cut the trail, and leeches become common.
In protected areas, collecting plants, animals and minerals and hunting may be prohibited.
Avoid hiking alone, always move with a guide, and tell your lodging your schedule.
Watch out for insects and snakes, and bring first-aid and everyday medicine.

to the west. The gateway city to western Panay, where you can combine museums, churches and a food trip.
A village on Iloilo's western coast and an old church town you can stop at on the way to Antique.
